summary: Extends the VPLS provider edge model to work with IEEE 802.1 Provider Backbone Bridging. PBB scales better than Provider Bridges in customer MAC addresses and service instances, and this document explains how VPLS can extend such services across an MPLS backbone.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains how to join two kinds of big shared-network systems so that very many users fit.

questions: how does pbb improve vpls scalability
subtitle: How to combine two big network technologies for better scalability.

tldr.problem: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) is widely deployed for Ethernet services across MPLS backbones, but it suffers from scalability limits as the number of customer services grows, because the core devices must track every customer MAC address and maintain pseudowires per service instance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows how to integrate IEEE Provider Backbone Bridges (PBB), which group customer MAC addresses under backbone MAC addresses, with VPLS. The combination uses PBB's two-level bridging (customer space and provider backbone space) within VPLS provider edge devices, reducing the number of MAC addresses and pseudowires in the core.
tldr.outcome: PBB-VPLS achieves better scalability in terms of the number of customer MAC addresses and service instances handled by core devices, while reusing existing VPLS control plane and signaling mechanisms.

today: RFC 7041 is an Informational RFC describing an architecture for improving VPLS scalability using PBB. The combination of PBB and VPLS (PBB-VPLS) continues to be used in service provider networks where high scalability is required. Later RFCs have built on this work to address specific signaling and OAM aspects.

sections.title: Two Technologies for Big Networks
sections.content:
VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service) makes a large MPLS backbone look like a single shared Ethernet, allowing multiple customer networks to send Ethernet frames through it without running spanning tree across the backbone. It is widely deployed in service provider networks.

PBB (Provider Backbone Bridges) is an IEEE standard that scales Ethernet networks by using a two-level addressing scheme: customer MAC addresses in the inner layer and provider MAC addresses in the outer layer. This allows the provider network to treat all customer frames with the same destination customer MAC as a single logical flow.

VPLS has scalability limits: as the number of customer service instances grows, core provider edge devices must track more customer MAC addresses and maintain more pseudowires (one per service instance to each other device). PBB offers a way to reduce these numbers by grouping customer traffic under provider backbone MACs.

This RFC shows how to combine PBB and VPLS so that a provider edge device acts as a PBB bridge, with customer-facing I-components (serving multiple customer sites) and a backbone-facing B-component (connected to the MPLS core via VPLS). The result is that the core sees fewer MAC addresses (provider backbone MACs instead of customer MACs) and maintains fewer pseudowires (one per backbone service instance instead of per customer instance).
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS is like a shared Ethernet across a big network, but it slows down when there are too many customers because each customer's address has to be remembered everywhere. PBB groups customer addresses under one provider address so the core network sees fewer addresses to remember.

sections.title: The PBB-VPLS Provider Edge Model
sections.content:
In a PBB-VPLS provider edge device, a bridge module acts as a PBB bridge with internal I-components and B-components. The bridge receives frames from customer edge devices at S-tagged service interfaces (carrying customer VLAN IDs and customer MAC addresses). Each I-component bridges customer frames and prepends PBB encapsulation (backbone MAC, backbone VLAN, and service instance ID). The B-component bridges these encapsulated frames based on backbone MAC addresses and forwards them toward the backbone.

The B-component connects to the MPLS backbone through virtual interfaces, which feed into VPLS Forwarders. These forwarders map incoming MPLS pseudowire labels to virtual B-component interfaces. This is the key insight: rather than having the bridge module talk directly to VPLS, the PW Forwarder acts as a bridge between the PBB bridge domain and the VPLS pseudowire mesh. Each PW corresponds to a backbone service instance (not a customer instance), drastically reducing the PW count.

The model reuses existing VPLS components and signaling: pseudowires are established using standard VPLS mechanisms (BGP auto-discovery and LDP label signaling, or BGP signaling), and each backbone service instance corresponds to one VPLS instance. The customer service instances (I-component level) can optionally be represented as separate VPLS instances for hierarchical control.
sections.plainLanguage: The PBB-VPLS provider edge has customer ports that connect to customers, an internal bridge that adds provider labels, and core ports that connect to the MPLS network. The core sees provider labels, not customer addresses, so it scales better.

sections.title: How Packets Flow Through PBB-VPLS
sections.content:
A customer frame arriving at an S-tagged service interface carries customer source and destination MAC addresses and a service VLAN ID. The I-component bridges it based on the customer MAC destination. If the frame exits toward the backbone, the I-component passes it to the B-component. The B-component encapsulates the frame with a provider backbone MAC header (adding source and destination provider MACs), a backbone VLAN tag (B-tag), and a service instance tag (I-tag that identifies which customer service this frame belongs to). This encapsulated frame is passed to a virtual interface connected to the PW Forwarder.

The PW Forwarder looks up which pseudowire to use for this backbone service instance (using the I-tag) and adds MPLS encapsulation (PSN header and PW label). The packet now travels across the backbone labeled with a single provider PW label.

At the far end, a PBB-VPLS PE receives the packet, removes MPLS encapsulation, and passes the PBB frame to the B-component. The B-component bridges based on the provider MAC destination address. If the frame exits toward customer interfaces, it reaches an I-component that removes the PBB encapsulation and delivers the original customer frame to the correct customer edge device.
sections.plainLanguage: Customer frames come in with customer addresses. The PE wraps them in provider addresses and an MPLS label. The backbone carries them using the provider label, not the customer address. At the far end, the PE unwraps them back to customer format.

sections.title: Control Plane and Signaling
sections.content:
PBB-VPLS reuses existing VPLS control plane mechanisms for setting up pseudowires and managing services. The procedures from RFC 4761 (BGP auto-discovery and signaling) and RFC 4762 (LDP signaling) apply directly. Each backbone service instance corresponds to one VPLS instance, and pseudowires are established in the normal VPLS fashion.

For customer-facing VPLS instances (in the I-component space), hierarchical VPLS (H-VPLS) procedures can optionally be used. This allows further scalability by reducing the number of pseudowires on customer-facing PEs.

No new signaling protocols or procedures are required; PBB-VPLS is a deployment architecture that extends existing VPLS mechanisms by running them above PBB bridges instead of directly on Ethernet ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The PBB-VPLS PE sets up pseudowires the same way regular VPLS does, using the same protocols. The only difference is that it uses PBB bridging inside the PE to group customer services.

sections.title: Multicast, Replication, and Operations
sections.content:
Packet replication (handling broadcast and multicast) is handled by the PBB bridge module, which floods unknown and multicast frames to appropriate interfaces. The existing VPLS hierarchy can be applied at both the customer (I-component) and backbone (B-component) levels to reduce redundant packet copying across the network. IGMP and PIM snooping can be applied per customer service instance to prevent multicast traffic from reaching non-member sites.

Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) procedures from both PBB and VPLS can be used. PBB uses IEEE Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) and ITU-T Y.1731 tools in both I-components and B-components for fault detection and performance monitoring. VPLS OAM (PW OAM and VPLS OAM) verifies connectivity at the pseudowire and service instance levels. Both sets of tools can be deployed together in a PBB-VPLS network.
sections.plainLanguage: When a customer sends broadcast or multicast frames, the PE floods them to all relevant customers. OAM tools (health checks) work at both the customer level and the provider backbone level.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that no new security issues are introduced by PBB-VPLS beyond those already addressed in the base VPLS RFCs (RFC 4761 and RFC 4762). The security model of VPLS applies: pseudowires are authenticated and encrypted using existing mechanisms, and per-VPLS forwarding isolation is maintained. The addition of PBB bridging inside the PE does not expose new attack surfaces at the protocol level, as PBB bridging is a local forwarding function.

Operators must ensure that the PBB bridge module itself is protected from tampering and that VPLS configuration is validated, just as in regular VPLS deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: PBB-VPLS does not add new security problems compared to regular VPLS. The same protections (encryption, authentication) apply.
